items.title: ELT's INSANE 39m MIRROR! #shorts
items.summary: Why do we need a telescope as large as 39m across? The bigger the telescope you have, the smaller the object you can see. And thanks to ELT’s size and its 6 giant lasers that can correct for the blurr…
items.body:
Why do we need a telescope as large as 39m across?

The bigger the telescope you have, the smaller the object you can see. And thanks to ELT’s size and its 6 giant lasers that can correct for the blurring of Earth’s atmosphere, ELT should be able to give us images that are 16 times sharper than Hubble, and 6 times sharper than JWST once it comes online in 2030.

But one single piece of glass 39m wide is not a good idea. It would be so heavy that it would bend under its own weight.

Instead engineers have developed ELT’s primary light collecting mirror to have 798 individual hexagonal segments each measuring 1.4 metres across.

That means installing ELT’s mirror is going to be one very large, nervous jigsaw puzzle.

That’s the job of the segment manipulator.

And to see that, we need to head to the heart of engineering at ESO, and get geared up.

Video filmed on a Sony ⍺7 IV

items.body:
The Space Shuttle glided to a runway. Falcon 9 lands on its engines. Super Heavy can even be caught by its launch tower. Why use three different methods? items.body:

In this Seestar S30 Plus review, I share my backyard astrophotography results and explain where it fits between the original Seestar S30 and S30 Pro.

After about a week of testing, I’ve captured the Andromeda Galaxy, Horsehead Nebula, and Sun, tried both alt-az and EQ mode, and explored the separate wide-angle camera. There’s plenty to like about this portable smart telescope, along with a few limitations to understand before buying.

The S30 Plus combines a telescope, cameras, automatic tracking, and live image stacking in one compact setup controlled from your phone. Its dual 2K cameras produce 1440 × 2560 images, offering more resolution than the original S30 while keeping the price below the S30 Pro.

In this video, I cover:

• Seestar S30 Plus vs. S30 vs. S30 Pro: what’s different?
• My deep-sky images and first impressions
• What “dual 2K imaging” actually means
• Alt-az vs. EQ mode and my preferred exposure length
• Choosing the built-in filter for galaxies and nebulae
• Wide-angle Milky Way, star-trail, and time-lapse modes
• Battery performance during cold, damp nights
• Storage, FITS files, and USB transfer quirks
• Solar imaging with the supplied solar filter

Death isn't a single switch that shuts down your entire body at once. When your heart stops beating and your brain goes silent, trillions of cells inside you are still alive, desperately trying to keep themselves running. Death isn't a single moment, but a slow and surprisingly complex process that can last for weeks.

What actually happens when you die? What makes death so mysterious, and which cells are the last survivors within your body?

items.body:
很多朋友可能第一次听到“大千干烧鱼”这个名字，这里的“大千”指的是国画大师张大千先生。张大千是四川内江人，不仅画画厉害，也非常懂吃、会做川菜。资料记载，大千干烧鱼是在传统川味烧鱼的基础上经过他的改良形成的。这道菜最大的特点就是“干烧”，不留很多汤汁，慢慢把汁水收浓，让味道都挂在鱼上面，吃起来干香浓郁，特别下饭。

鲤鱼（1条）

items.title: Seeing parts of the ELT get built! #shorts
items.summary: Building the 39m wide extremely large telescope in the Chilean desert is no easy feat. Getting it to actually work is even harder. So I’ve come to the Headquarters of the European Southern Observatory…
items.body:
Building the 39m wide extremely large telescope in the Chilean desert is no easy feat. Getting it to actually work is even harder.

So I’ve come to the Headquarters of the European Southern Observatory in Garching, for a behind-the-scenes sneak peak at the machinery that will allow the ELT to capture spectacular images of our night sky and make the next generation of astrophysics research possible.

With a mirror 39m across, ELT will be 4 times larger than the largest telescope we’ve ever built, collecting 100 million times more light than the human eye.

But whilst a telescope's massive main light collecting mirror normally gets all the glory, under the hood there are thousands of unbelievable feats of engineering ingenuity to make all of this possible, and to record the light the telescope collects.

And sometimes, you just have to see it to believe it!

Video filmed on a Sony ⍺7 IV

items.title: How to see the planetary parade in November 2026 #shorts
items.summary: It’s this steady rise of Venus higher in the morning sky through November, and Mercury behind it lower on the sky, that will give us the so-called planet parade. I’ll warn you now, you’re going to see…
items.body:
It’s this steady rise of Venus higher in the morning sky through November, and Mercury behind it lower on the sky, that will give us the so-called planet parade.

I’ll warn you now, you’re going to see a lot of hype online about the planet parade, with some people even calling it a planetary alignment and I just want to set expectations.

Because yes it’s incredibly cool that you can see Jupiter, Mars and Venus, and possibly mercury if you have a flat horizon, in the sky at the same time, in the mornings just before sunrise.

And yes they will all roughly be aligned, because the solar system is flat and all the planets orbit in the same plane around the Sun, so all take roughly the same path through the sky.

But Jupiter and Mars will be close together, high in the sky, and then bright Venus nearer the horizon, with fainter Mercury really hard to spot below it. So most people are only going to be able to spot 3 planets. And they won’t look like they’re in a straight line.

You’ll hear most people saying this is going to happen around the 18th November, because that’s when Mercury reaches its highest point, but since most people won’t be able to see Mercury anyway because of trees and buildings in the way, anytime from early November is good for this.

In fact the more mornings you can spot the positions of the planets this month the better, because bright Jupiter and reddish Mars will slowly be getting closer and closer together in the sky from our perspective here on Earth as they move along their orbits.

They reach their closest pass on the 15th November, before they start to move apart again. And their close pass will be fun to see, but it’s also more rewarding if you’ve done your astronomy homework and watched them get closer and closer over the next few weeks.

items.title: NOT a singularity: an infinitely thin donut! #shorts
items.summary: This is where you need to tear up everything you think you know about black holes. Because for a rotating black hole, you don’t have a singularity, you have a ring singularity. An infinitely thin donu…
items.body:
This is where you need to tear up everything you think you know about black holes.

Because for a rotating black hole, you don’t have a singularity, you have a ring singularity. An infinitely thin donut. That’s because of the forces at play because the black hole is spinning, throwing the matter outwards.

It’s a similar process to what you feel holding hands with a friend and spinning around. You feel thrown backwards. It’s what makes Earth not a perfect sphere but an oblate spheroid, slightly squashed and bulging at the equator. Saturn spinning faster is even more squashed. Take that to the extreme for black holes and you end up with a ring shaped singularity. That some people like to portmanteau and call a ringularity. Those people are psychos.

Video filmed on a Sony ⍺7 IV
Video edited by Martino Gasparrini: martino.freelance@gmail.com
